title: Proxy & Reflect: Trapping [[Get]], [[Set]], and Engine Invariants

progressiveExplaining.eli5: Imagine a security guard at a building's front desk. Everyone who wants to visit the building must check in with the guard first — the guard decides whether to allow the visit, change the visitor's destination, or silently keep a record. But the guard must follow strict rules: he can never claim a room is empty if the real building says someone lives there, and he can never pretend a locked door is open. In JavaScript, a Proxy is that guard around a thing: every request to read or change a property passes through the guard's rules, but the guard must always tell the truth about the fixed properties of the real thing.
progressiveExplaining.junior: A Proxy wraps an object (the target) and lets you intercept operations via traps: get, set, has, deleteProperty, ownKeys, apply, construct, and more. const p = new Proxy(target, { get(obj, key) { return key in obj ? obj[key] : 'missing'; } });. Reflect provides the default behavior as plain functions: Reflect.get(target, key) does the standard lookup, and calling it inside a trap avoids infinite recursion. Use Proxies for validation, logging, observability (like Vue's reactivity), memoization, and mocking. Note: a proxy does NOT change the target — traps are added behavior around it. Proxies are slower than plain objects, so use them where interception is the feature, not on every hot path.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, Proxies intercept the internal methods of the object model — [[Get]], [[Set]], [[HasProperty]], [[OwnPropertyKeys]], [[GetPrototypeOf]], [[DefineOwnProperty]], etc. Reflect mirrors these exact operations as callable functions, so forwarding all traps through Reflect preserves default semantics, including receiver binding for getters and strict-mode behavior. The crucial design property is the invariant system: a trap result that violates an object's fixed attributes (e.g. reporting a non-configurable, non-writable property as absent) throws a TypeError. This is why Proxies cannot fully lie about invariants, making them safe for engine optimizations (though they do force deoptimization to the slow path).
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: When V8 sees a proxy as the receiver of an operation, it dispatches to a runtime/slow path that calls the matching trap instead of the fast Map-based property path. get traps must call [[Get]] on the target to verify invariants: for a non-configurable, non-writable data property, the trap must return the exact same value; for a non-configurable accessor without a setter, the trap must return undefined. The ownKeys trap must include all non-configurable own keys and must not include keys the target does not have (unless the target has no non-configurable keys). Reflect.* functions are specified to invoke the same internal methods, so Reflect.get(target, key, receiver) forwards receiver — critical for getters whose this should be the proxy, not the target.

rosettaStone.react: React dev tools and state libs use proxies to instrument component state; production hot paths avoid proxies for speed.
rosettaStone.angular: Zone.js patches rather than proxies most internals, but Angular's zoneless experiments use signal-based (non-proxy) reactivity.
rosettaStone.vue: Vue 3 reactivity IS proxy-based: reactive() wraps objects and intercepts get/set/has/ownKeys to track and trigger effects.
rosettaStone.svelte: Svelte 5 runes use compiler-driven signals rather than proxies — compiled access, not runtime interception.

codeComparison.title: Naive forwarding trap vs correct Reflect-forwarding trap with receiver
codeComparison.summary: Hand-rolling get traps with target[key] breaks getter receiver binding; forwarding through Reflect preserves correct this semantics.

legacyOrBad.label: Manual forwarding without receiver
legacyOrBad.snippet: get(target, key) { return target[key]; } // ❌ OLD: breaks getter `this` — getters see target, not proxy

modernOrGood.label: Reflect.get with receiver forwarding
modernOrGood.snippet: get(target, key, receiver) { return Reflect.get(target, key, receiver); } // ✅ NEW: getters see the proxy

interviewGotchas.question: Why must a get trap return the exact same value for a non-configurable, non-writable property, and what happens if it doesn't?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This probes your understanding of proxy invariants — the hard contract that keeps proxies from corrupting the object model and lets engines trust object metadata.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: A non-configurable, non-writable own data property on the target is fixed: no operation may change or conceal its value without violating the object's invariant. The get trap's result is checked against the target: the engine calls [[Get]] on the target, and if the property is a non-configurable, non-writable data property, the trap must return exactly that value. Violating this throws a TypeError. This invariant protects engine invariants (e.g. shape/Map assumptions) and guarantees that a proxy cannot masquerade as having a different value for a permanently fixed property, which would otherwise break spec-guaranteed behaviors like constant folding.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'the proxy can return anything it wants because it is a proxy'. Invariants forbid lying about non-configurable properties, including non-configurable accessors (get must be undefined if no setter), ownKeys must include non-configurable keys, and getPrototypeOf must return the target's actual non-extensible prototype. Another trap: assuming the invariant check is optional — engines enforce it with a TypeError, so violating it is a hard crash, not a silent fallback.

interviewGotchas.question: What is the difference between proxy.get(target, key) and Reflect.get(target, key, receiver)?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Interviewers ask this to see whether you understand receiver semantics and why naive trap forwarding is subtly broken for accessors.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Reflect.get(target, key, receiver) executes the exact [[Get]] internal method with an explicit receiver — the `this` used when evaluating an accessor (getter) found during the lookup. A bare target[key] inside a get trap performs a plain property access with this bound to target, so getters run against the raw target instead of the proxy: proxy-internal state is invisible to them, and any chained property reads bypass your traps. Forwarding receiver is essential for correct proxy composition — Vue's reactive, for example, forwards receiver so nested getters observe the reactive wrapper. For data properties there is no difference; the difference only manifests with accessors and inherited getters.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'they are identical for property reads'. They diverge precisely when an accessor is encountered on the prototype or target. Another trap: forgetting that Reflect functions exist for every trap and are the canonical forwarder — hand-rolling forwarding with target[key] or target[key] = v subtly breaks receiver/this, strict mode, and invariant checks. Candidates who reach for Reflect.* by default show they know the contract.
